study_guide.title: 1. Access Modifiers
study_guide.content:
Four levels, from most closed to most open:
| Modifier | Same class | Same package | Subclass (other package) | Anywhere |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `private` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| *(none)* — package-private | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `protected` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `public` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

**Default to `private`**: Every public field is an irrevocable API promise. `private` fields + deliberate public methods keep internals safe.

study_guide.title: 2. Constructor Overloading
study_guide.content: Several constructors distinguished by parameter types. Avoid duplicate field initialization in multiple constructor bodies — it causes silent field initialization bugs during refactoring.

study_guide.title: 3. Constructor Chaining with this(...)
study_guide.content:
Use `this(...)` to delegate from overloaded constructors to a single canonical constructor.
- `this(...)` must be the **very first statement** in the constructor.
- `this(...)` goes sideways (same class); `super(...)` goes upward (parent class).

study_guide.title: 4. final on a Variable
study_guide.content:
Assigned once, never reassigned.
**`final` freezes the reference, not the object's contents.** `final List<String> list` prevents reassigning `list`, but `list.add(...)` is still permitted.

study_guide.title: 5. final on a Method
study_guide.content: Prevents subclasses from overriding the method. Critical for identity accessors (e.g. `getDriverId()`) to preserve the integrity of `equals()` and `hashCode()`.

study_guide.title: 6. final on a Class
study_guide.content: Seals the class so no other class can extend it. `java.lang.String` is `final` to ensure immutability cannot be undermined by a mutable subclass.

study_guide.title: 7. The Immutability Pattern
study_guide.content:
Three required ingredients:
1. Every field is `final`
2. No setter methods
3. The class itself is `final`
To update an immutable object, return a new instance (e.g., `withSurge(...)`, `String.toUpperCase()`).

study_guide.title: 8. Inheritance with extends
study_guide.content: Declares an **IS-A** relationship. Parent methods run child overrides dynamically at runtime (**dynamic dispatch**).

study_guide.title: 9. super(...) and Construction Order
study_guide.content: Parent constructor always executes before the child constructor body. If omitted, Java inserts an implicit `super()` call.

study_guide.title: 10. protected in its Natural Habitat
study_guide.content: Allows members to be accessible to subclasses and the same package, but closed to external callers. Prefer protected *methods* over protected *fields*.

study_guide.title: 11. Shallow Copy Pitfall
study_guide.content: Copying object references copies memory addresses rather than the underlying state. Mutating a shallow-copied object mutates the original object.

study_guide.title: 12. Deep Copy & Copy Constructors
study_guide.content:
Rule: **Mutable field -> Deep copy (new object); Immutable field -> Share the reference.**
Apply defensive copying both on input into constructors and on output via getters.

study_guide.title: 13. The Object Class & @Override
study_guide.content: All classes inherit from `java.lang.Object`. Always annotate method overrides with `@Override` so the compiler catches mismatched parameter types.

study_guide.title: 14. == vs equals()
study_guide.content:
`==` compares memory addresses for objects. `equals()` defines semantic equality.
The 5 rules of `equals()`: Reflexive, Symmetric, Transitive, Consistent, Null-safe.
Use `getClass() != obj.getClass()` to ensure strict symmetry across subclasses.

study_guide.title: 15. The hashCode Contract & HashMap
study_guide.content:
If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` MUST be true.
`hashCode()` selects the HashMap bucket; `equals()` disambiguates keys inside the bucket. Never include mutable fields in `hashCode()`.

expanded_modules.title: Databases & SQL
expanded_modules.description: Relational modeling, query design, transactions, and production data access for backend systems.

lessons.title: Introduction to DBMS & Keys
lessons.description: Tables, relationships, constraints, and key design.
lessons.concepts: A DBMS is responsible for durable storage, concurrency control, recovery, and query execution; an application should still make ownership and invariants explicit. Compare natural, surrogate, primary, candidate, and foreign keys, and understand why a constraint is stronger than a validation performed only in application code.
lessons.scenario: Model a booking system with customers, events, seats, and reservations. The database must prevent two reservations for the same event-seat pair even when two API instances race.
lessons.practice: Draw the entity relationships, declare keys and constraints, insert valid and invalid rows, and explain which invariant belongs in the database.
lessons.evidence: You can choose keys from identity and lifecycle needs, explain referential integrity, and show a database constraint rejecting an invalid booking.
lessons.extension: Add a soft-delete policy and explain how it affects uniqueness, foreign keys, and historical reporting.

lessons.title: CRUD Operations - 1
lessons.description: Insert, update, delete, and select operations with safe parameters.
lessons.concepts: CRUD is not merely syntax: predicates, null semantics, affected-row counts, and parameter binding determine correctness. A command should state whether zero matching rows is an error, a no-op, or an idempotent retry.
lessons.scenario: Implement a customer profile update endpoint using parameterized SQL. A retry should not accidentally update every customer because a filter was omitted.
lessons.practice: Write parameterized inserts and updates, test null and duplicate cases, inspect affected-row counts, and make a delete policy explicit.
lessons.evidence: You can distinguish a safe command from an unsafe string-built query and define the outcome of repeated updates and deletes.
lessons.extension: Add an audit table and record the actor and reason without placing credentials or raw SQL in logs.

lessons.title: CRUD Operations - 2
lessons.description: Pagination, ordering, null handling, and reliable write responses.
lessons.concepts: Production CRUD needs deterministic ordering, bounded result sets, and a clear response after a write. Offset pagination is simple but can drift under inserts; keyset pagination trades arbitrary page jumps for stable traversal.
lessons.scenario: Build an order-history query that remains stable while new orders arrive. Return a cursor based on created time and id so a client can resume without duplicates.
lessons.practice: Implement offset and keyset versions, add a compound sort, test ties and null values, and compare the query plan for a large result set.
lessons.evidence: You can explain why `ORDER BY` is required for deterministic pagination and choose a cursor that is unique and opaque to the client.
lessons.extension: Add an export job with a repeatable snapshot boundary and document how late-arriving records are handled.

lessons.title: Joins
lessons.description: Inner, outer, semi, and anti-joins for relational data.
lessons.concepts: Joins express how rows from different relations combine. The join predicate, null behavior, and cardinality determine whether the result is complete, duplicated, or silently filtered.
lessons.scenario: Return a booking list with customer name, event title, payment state, and optional refund information. A left join must retain bookings that have no refund.
lessons.practice: Write inner, left, and anti-join queries, inspect duplicate rows, and verify the expected row count with deliberately missing relationships.
lessons.evidence: You can choose a join from the business question, identify accidental fan-out, and explain why a filter in `WHERE` can change an outer join into an inner one.
lessons.extension: Refactor a large join into a read model when the endpoint has a stable high-volume access pattern.

lessons.title: Aggregate Queries
lessons.description: GROUP BY, HAVING, nulls, and metric correctness.
lessons.concepts: Aggregations turn events into business measures, but the grouping grain must be explicit. Count rows only when row multiplicity is understood, and distinguish `count(*)`, `count(column)`, and distinct counts.
lessons.scenario: Produce daily payment totals by merchant while excluding test transactions and separating authorized from settled amounts.
lessons.practice: State the metric grain, write grouped queries, add `HAVING` thresholds, test empty groups and nulls, and reconcile the result with a hand-calculated sample.
lessons.evidence: You can identify double counting caused by joins and explain why a metric needs a documented grain and filter policy.
lessons.extension: Materialize a daily summary and compare its refresh strategy with computing the aggregate at request time.

lessons.title: Joins and Aggregate Queries Working Session
lessons.description: Combining joins and aggregates without changing the metric grain.
lessons.concepts: This working session focuses on query reasoning: establish the base relation, join one relationship at a time, and aggregate only after deciding whether the join multiplies facts. Pre-aggregation or distinct keys may be required.
lessons.scenario: Calculate average delivery time per city from orders, deliveries, and driver assignments without counting an order once per status event.
lessons.practice: Write the query in stages, inspect intermediate row counts, add a counterexample, and compare a correlated query with a pre-aggregated subquery.
lessons.evidence: You can defend every row in the final result and find a double-counting bug by checking intermediate cardinality.
lessons.extension: Create a small query test fixture that fails when a future schema change changes the metric grain.

lessons.title: Subqueries & Views
lessons.description: Correlated subqueries, common table expressions, and views.
lessons.concepts: A subquery can express existence, ranking, or a derived relation. Common table expressions improve readability, while views expose a stable read contract; neither automatically makes a query fast or materialized.
lessons.scenario: Expose the latest successful payment per order and hide provider-specific columns behind a view used by support tooling.
lessons.practice: Implement `EXISTS`, a scalar subquery, and a CTE; compare their plans; create a view with an explicit ownership and change policy.
lessons.evidence: You can choose a subquery based on the question, explain correlation cost, and treat a view as an API with compatibility expectations.
lessons.extension: Add a materialized view for a measured reporting workload and document refresh staleness.

lessons.title: Indexing
lessons.description: B-tree access, composite indexes, selectivity, and query plans.
lessons.concepts: An index is a write and storage trade-off that supports a particular access pattern. Column order, equality and range predicates, sort order, partial predicates, and data distribution all influence whether the planner can use it.
lessons.scenario: Speed up a support query for a tenant's recent failed payments without making every insert pay for an unnecessary index.
lessons.practice: Capture a baseline with `EXPLAIN`, add the smallest useful index, measure again, and test a query that does not match the index prefix.
lessons.evidence: You can tie an index to a concrete query shape and explain why an index may be ignored or make writes slower.
lessons.extension: Review unused indexes from production statistics and propose a safe removal process with rollback evidence.

lessons.title: Transactions
lessons.description: Atomicity, isolation, locks, retries, and transaction boundaries.
lessons.concepts: A transaction defines which changes succeed together and what concurrent work may observe. Isolation is a business trade-off: stronger guarantees can increase waiting, while weaker isolation requires conflict handling.
lessons.scenario: Reserve the last inventory unit and create an order atomically. A timeout must not leave a reservation that the user cannot see or release.
lessons.practice: Run two concurrent transactions, observe a conflict, choose an isolation level, and make the retry or user-visible failure behavior explicit.
lessons.evidence: You can identify the transaction boundary, explain a lock wait, and distinguish a database retry from blindly repeating a side effect.
lessons.extension: Add an outbox row in the same transaction and design a publisher that can safely retry delivery.

lessons.title: Window Functions
lessons.description: Ranking, running totals, partitions, and frame semantics.
lessons.concepts: Window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing the result set. Partition, order, and frame clauses are separate decisions; a default frame can surprise a cumulative metric when values tie.
lessons.scenario: Show each merchant's payment with its running settled total, previous payment, and rank within the merchant's day.
lessons.practice: Implement `row_number`, `lag`, and a running sum, test ties and partitions, and verify the frame against a manually calculated example.
lessons.evidence: You can select a window function instead of a self-join and explain how partitioning and framing affect the result.
lessons.extension: Use a window query to identify late-arriving events and feed a reconciliation report.

lessons.title: Schema Design - 1
lessons.description: Normalization, aggregates, ownership, and lifecycle modeling.
lessons.concepts: Schema design starts with business facts and update rules. Normalize data that changes independently, keep derived values deliberate, and model state transitions so invalid combinations are difficult to store.
lessons.scenario: Design a ride-booking schema that separates a ride request, assignment, payment attempt, and driver location while preserving historical facts.
lessons.practice: Write the functional dependencies, normalize the first draft, identify aggregate boundaries, and choose which values are snapshots versus references.
lessons.evidence: You can explain why a table exists, what one row means, and which changes must be atomic.
lessons.extension: Review the model for tenant isolation, retention, auditability, and migration cost before adding indexes.

lessons.title: Schema Design - 2
lessons.description: Denormalization, partitioning, constraints, and migration-ready design.
lessons.concepts: Denormalization is justified by measured reads, not by fear of joins. Store derived data with a refresh or correction path, use constraints for invariants, and plan schema changes for old and new application versions.
lessons.scenario: Design an order-event table that can serve customer history and operational analytics while growing by millions of rows per day.
lessons.practice: Compare normalized and read-optimized models, choose a partition key, write a backfill plan, and test dual-read or dual-write compatibility.
lessons.evidence: You can defend a denormalization decision with a workload, consistency model, and repair strategy.
lessons.extension: Simulate a rolling deployment where the old API and new API both read the schema safely.

lessons.title: Databases & SQL Contest: SQL and Schema Design
lessons.description: Timed query reasoning, schema choices, and production trade-offs.
lessons.concepts: The contest evaluates whether you can turn an ambiguous backend requirement into a clear grain, schema, query, constraint, and performance plan. Correctness comes before clever SQL.
lessons.scenario: Build the data layer for a marketplace with merchants, orders, refunds, inventory, and daily settlement while handling duplicate events and late corrections.
lessons.practice: Clarify assumptions, sketch the schema, implement the highest-value queries, add constraints, inspect plans, and record unresolved trade-offs.
lessons.evidence: You can explain every table and query, prove the important invariants, and identify what must be measured before launch.
lessons.extension: Write a short review of the design as if handing it to an on-call engineer, including rollback and reconciliation steps.

expanded_modules.title: High-Level Design
expanded_modules.description: Distributed-system fundamentals, scalable infrastructure, data platforms, and AI-aware system design.

lessons.title: System Design Foundations & Modern Infrastructure
lessons.description: Requirements, capacity, boundaries, and architecture trade-offs.
lessons.concepts: HLD starts with user journeys, scale assumptions, consistency needs, and failure budgets. Components should follow ownership and workload rather than fashionable technology names.
lessons.scenario: Design a multi-tenant document platform from request volume, object sizes, latency targets, and retention requirements.
lessons.practice: Write functional and non-functional requirements, estimate rough capacity, draw the first architecture, and list the riskiest assumptions.
lessons.evidence: You can communicate an architecture from requirements and identify what must be measured before choosing a technology.
lessons.extension: Add a cost and operational review to the design record.

lessons.title: Load Balancing, Consistent Hashing & Traffic Routing at Scale
lessons.description: Routing, health, stickiness, hashing, and failover.
lessons.concepts: Load balancing distributes work while preserving the state and locality guarantees a system needs. Consistent hashing reduces movement during membership changes but does not solve hot keys or unhealthy nodes by itself.
lessons.scenario: Route requests for tenants and documents across service replicas while keeping a cache key near its data when helpful.
lessons.practice: Compare round robin, least-loaded, and hash-based routing; model node removal; and define health and retry behavior.
lessons.evidence: You can explain why a routing choice affects cache locality, failover, and hot-spot risk.
lessons.extension: Add a hot-key mitigation strategy and a controlled zone failure test.

lessons.title: Caching Systems: CDN, Backend Caches, Cache Invalidation
lessons.description: Cache layers, TTL, invalidation, and stale-data policy.
lessons.concepts: Caching is a consistency decision. Define what may be stale, who invalidates it, how misses behave, and how memory pressure or a cache outage affects the source of truth.
lessons.scenario: Serve public document metadata through a CDN and tenant-scoped search results through a backend cache without leaking private data.
lessons.practice: Choose keys and TTLs, model cache-aside behavior, test invalidation and stampede control, and define cache outage behavior.
lessons.evidence: You can state the freshness contract and identify a cache key that would be unsafe.
lessons.extension: Add request coalescing and measure hit rate, staleness, and origin load.

lessons.title: Case Study: Caching at Scale
lessons.description: Cache design for judge, leaderboard, and AI workload patterns.
lessons.concepts: High-read systems have different cache shapes: a leaderboard may need sorted updates, a code judge needs result isolation, and an AI workload may need semantic or response caching with careful privacy boundaries.
lessons.scenario: Design caches for contest rankings and repeated model prompts, including invalidation when a submission or prompt version changes.
lessons.practice: Map keys, write paths, TTLs, and consistency needs for each workload; identify what cannot be shared across tenants.
lessons.evidence: You can explain why one cache policy cannot be copied across all read-heavy features.
lessons.extension: Add a stampede test and a cost comparison between recomputation and cached responses.

lessons.title: Case Study: Caching Facebook News Feed
lessons.description: Fan-out choices, feed ranking, and freshness.
lessons.concepts: A feed design balances write amplification, read latency, ranking freshness, and celebrity or hot-user effects. Fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read are workload choices, not universal rules.
lessons.scenario: Design a personalized activity feed where a small set of publishers has millions of followers and AI ranking is an optional layer.
lessons.practice: Estimate fan-out work, choose a hybrid strategy, define cache invalidation, and handle a ranking service timeout.
lessons.evidence: You can explain what is precomputed, what is assembled on read, and how a hot publisher is contained.
lessons.extension: Add a backfill or replay plan when the ranking model version changes.

lessons.title: CAP/PACELC Theorem + Master-Slave Replication
lessons.description: Consistency, availability, latency, and replication lag.
lessons.concepts: Distributed systems make trade-offs under partition and normal operation. CAP describes a partition scenario; PACELC adds the latency-versus-consistency decision when the network is healthy. Replication lag must be visible to product behavior.
lessons.scenario: A customer reads order status from a replica immediately after writing through the primary.
lessons.practice: State the read-after-write requirement, choose routing or session guarantees, and define what stale data the UI can show.
lessons.evidence: You can avoid treating CAP as a database product label and describe the user-visible compromise.
lessons.extension: Add a lag-aware read policy and an alert threshold.

lessons.title: SQL vs NoSQL + Sharding
lessons.description: Data models, partition keys, and operational trade-offs.
lessons.concepts: Choose a data model from access patterns, invariants, query flexibility, and operational needs. Sharding can improve scale but makes transactions, queries, rebalancing, and cross-shard uniqueness harder.
lessons.scenario: Store tenant documents and processing events where tenant isolation, time-based queries, and per-document state are important.
lessons.practice: Compare a relational and a key-value model, choose a partition key, and list cross-partition operations that need a redesign.
lessons.evidence: You can defend the choice without claiming that one database family is universally superior.
lessons.extension: Design a resharding and hot-tenant mitigation plan.

lessons.title: Database Orchestration & Shard Creation
lessons.description: Shard lifecycle, placement, migrations, and routing metadata.
lessons.concepts: Shards are an operational system: placement, capacity, ownership, schema version, and routing must be managed. A new shard should become usable through a controlled workflow, not a manual mystery step.
lessons.scenario: Provision a tenant shard, copy or initialize schema, update routing, and roll back if health checks fail.
lessons.practice: Define shard metadata, create a state machine, handle partial provisioning, and test a routing update during traffic.
lessons.evidence: You can explain how a request finds a shard and how operators recover from a half-created shard.
lessons.extension: Add a rebalancing plan with dual-read or migration checkpoints.

lessons.title: Case Study: Google Typeahead - How to Approach System Design Problems
lessons.description: Latency goals, query shaping, indexing, and ranking requirements.
lessons.concepts: A typeahead design begins with keystroke rate, prefix distribution, result freshness, response budget, and language requirements. The architecture follows those constraints.
lessons.scenario: Design autocomplete for products and documents with prefix matching, typo tolerance, tenant filters, and a strict response deadline.
lessons.practice: Estimate query volume, define the index, decide update latency, and write the fallback for an unavailable search tier.
lessons.evidence: You can turn a vague autocomplete prompt into measurable requirements and a staged design.
lessons.extension: Add an evaluation set for relevance and latency by prefix frequency.

lessons.title: Case Study: Google Typeahead - Design and Optimizations
lessons.description: Caching prefixes, compression, ranking, and incremental updates.
lessons.concepts: Optimization should target a measured bottleneck. Popular prefixes may be cached, indexes may be compressed, and ranking can be tiered, but every shortcut has freshness or memory cost.
lessons.scenario: Reduce p95 latency for common prefixes while keeping new products searchable within a defined freshness window.
lessons.practice: Measure a baseline, add one optimization at a time, test hot prefixes and cold misses, and document the capacity impact.
lessons.evidence: You can connect each optimization to a metric and explain its failure behavior.
lessons.extension: Add admission control so a flood of unique prefixes does not evict useful entries.

lessons.title: NoSQL Internals - LSM Tree and Multi-Master
lessons.description: Write paths, compaction, conflict resolution, and read amplification.
lessons.concepts: LSM-based systems trade write behavior for compaction and read amplification. Multi-master replication improves write locality and availability but requires explicit conflict resolution and convergence semantics.
lessons.scenario: Store high-volume event writes and tolerate regional connectivity gaps while preserving idempotent event identity.
lessons.practice: Trace memtable, log, SSTable, and compaction behavior conceptually; define a conflict key and resolution rule.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the operational cost behind the write throughput headline.
lessons.extension: Add tombstone-retention and compaction-pressure signals to an operations plan.

lessons.title: Case Study: Messaging Apps
lessons.description: Conversation ordering, delivery, presence, and fan-out.
lessons.concepts: Messaging systems need a clear ordering scope, delivery semantics, durable history, and presence that is allowed to be approximate. User experience should reflect pending, delivered, and failed states.
lessons.scenario: Design direct and group messaging with offline devices, retries, attachments, and AI-assisted summaries that cannot reorder the source conversation.
lessons.practice: Define message ids and ordering, choose storage and queue boundaries, and model reconnect and duplicate delivery.
lessons.evidence: You can explain what ordering is guaranteed and how a client reconciles after reconnect.
lessons.extension: Add retention and abuse controls without coupling moderation to message delivery correctness.

lessons.title: Messaging Queues - Apache Kafka & Zookeeper
lessons.description: Partitions, keys, consumer groups, offsets, and rebalancing.
lessons.concepts: Kafka provides an ordered log per partition and replayable offsets. Partition keys determine ordering and parallelism, while consumers must handle duplicates and reprocessing.
lessons.scenario: Publish order and document-processing events so independent consumers build search, notifications, and audit views.
lessons.practice: Choose keys, model consumer groups, handle offset commits and poison messages, and define replay safety.
lessons.evidence: You can explain partition-scoped ordering and why a consumer cannot assume exactly-once business effects without idempotency.
lessons.extension: Add an outbox and a lag-based alert.

lessons.title: Case Study: Elasticsearch - Full Text Search
lessons.description: Inverted indexes, analyzers, relevance, and operational search limits.
lessons.concepts: Search indexes are derived views. Choose analyzers and fields from language and query needs, keep source-of-truth data elsewhere, and define refresh and reindex behavior.
lessons.scenario: Index tenant documents for keyword and semantic-assisted search while applying authorization filters before returning results.
lessons.practice: Design mappings, analyzers, query clauses, refresh expectations, and a reindex plan for a changed schema.
lessons.evidence: You can explain why a search result is not the authoritative document and how deleted or restricted data is removed.
lessons.extension: Add relevance and authorization regression tests.

lessons.title: Case Study: S3 and HDFS - Large File Storage
lessons.description: Object storage, distributed file systems, multipart transfer, and metadata.
lessons.concepts: Large-file systems separate metadata from bytes and optimize for throughput, durability, and parallel access. Object stores have different consistency and namespace behavior from a filesystem.
lessons.scenario: Store uploaded documents and derived artifacts with tenant isolation, checksums, lifecycle retention, and resumable uploads.
lessons.practice: Define object keys, metadata, multipart boundaries, access controls, and recovery after a partial upload.
lessons.evidence: You can choose object storage or a distributed filesystem from access and processing needs.
lessons.extension: Add a garbage-collection job for abandoned multipart uploads.

lessons.title: Case Study: Uber - Nearest Neighbor Search
lessons.description: Geo-partitioning, indexing, freshness, and dispatch constraints.
lessons.concepts: Nearest-neighbor systems trade exactness, update cost, and latency. Dispatch also needs availability, fairness, and concurrency controls beyond finding the closest coordinate.
lessons.scenario: Find eligible drivers near a pickup while respecting vehicle type, current assignment, tenant or region, and stale location data.
lessons.practice: Choose a spatial index, define freshness, filter eligibility, and handle a driver becoming unavailable between search and assignment.
lessons.evidence: You can distinguish candidate search from the authoritative assignment transaction.
lessons.extension: Add a hot-zone strategy and a metric for rejected stale candidates.

lessons.title: Case Study: Rate Limiter + Unique ID Generator
lessons.description: Quotas, algorithms, coordination, and globally safe identity.
lessons.concepts: Rate limiting is a product and reliability policy. Token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, and sliding window have different burst and storage behavior. Unique ids need collision, ordering, and region considerations.
lessons.scenario: Protect a model API by tenant and endpoint while generating request ids that remain unique across replicas and regions.
lessons.practice: Choose a limit algorithm, define fail-open or fail-closed behavior, and compare UUID, database, and time-sortable id strategies.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the consistency needed for a quota and the operational effect of a limiter outage.
lessons.extension: Add a dry-run mode and quota headers for clients.

lessons.title: Case Study: OTT Platform
lessons.description: Catalog, playback, CDN, entitlements, and adaptive delivery.
lessons.concepts: An OTT design separates control-plane metadata from high-bandwidth media delivery. CDN placement, encoding, entitlement checks, and playback telemetry have different freshness and scaling needs.
lessons.scenario: Serve a video catalog with regional rights, adaptive streams, subscriptions, and AI-generated recommendations without putting media bytes through the application tier.
lessons.practice: Draw control and data paths, define caching and entitlement checks, and identify what happens when the recommendation service is down.
lessons.evidence: You can explain where scale comes from and which consistency compromises the viewer can tolerate.
lessons.extension: Add a playback QoE metric and a multi-CDN failover policy.

lessons.title: Microservices - 1
lessons.description: Service boundaries, data ownership, contracts, and workflow choice.
lessons.concepts: Microservices require independent ownership and deployment value. Each service should own its data and expose a contract; cross-service workflows need explicit orchestration or choreography and failure states.
lessons.scenario: Split a marketplace into order, payment, inventory, and notification capabilities only when their release or scaling needs justify the cost.
lessons.practice: Map bounded contexts, write APIs and events, identify distributed transactions, and compare a modular monolith with service decomposition.
lessons.evidence: You can defend a boundary and name the operational costs it introduces.
lessons.extension: Design an incremental extraction with compatibility and rollback checkpoints.

lessons.title: Microservices - 2
lessons.description: Observability, resilience, deployment, and data consistency across services.
lessons.concepts: A distributed system needs trace context, stable error contracts, idempotent consumers, deadlines, and deployment compatibility. Eventual consistency must be visible to users and operators.
lessons.scenario: Operate a document workflow across intake, extraction, indexing, and notification services during a provider outage and a rolling deployment.
lessons.practice: Add trace spans, retries with budgets, a dead-letter path, contract compatibility, and a reconciliation process.
lessons.evidence: You can trace a failed request, explain its partial state, and identify a safe recovery action.
lessons.extension: Write a service-level objective and an incident runbook for the most likely dependency failure.

lessons.title: Case Study: Ecommerce Platform (Microservices)
lessons.description: Catalog, cart, checkout, inventory, payments, orders, and asynchronous workflows.
lessons.concepts: An ecommerce platform is a useful microservices exercise because its domains have different consistency and scaling needs. Catalog browsing can tolerate cached or eventually consistent reads, while inventory reservation, payment authorization, and order state require explicit invariants, idempotency, and auditable transitions. Events connect the workflow, but each service must remain authoritative for its own state.
lessons.scenario: Design a multi-tenant ecommerce platform where a customer browses a catalog, adds an item to a cart, checks out, and receives an order confirmation while inventory is contested and a payment provider may retry or time out.
lessons.practice: Define bounded contexts and ownership, estimate traffic for browse versus checkout, model the order saga, add idempotency keys and an outbox, choose synchronous versus asynchronous calls, and test duplicate requests, reservation expiry, payment uncertainty, and compensating actions.
lessons.evidence: You can explain which operations require strong coordination, how an order moves through states, how duplicate events are made harmless, and how operators recover an order stuck between payment and fulfillment.
lessons.extension: Add regional traffic routing, inventory oversell protection, contract-versioned events, fraud review, and an SLO dashboard covering checkout success, reservation latency, payment reconciliation, and fulfillment lag.

expanded_modules.title: Data Engineering
expanded_modules.description: Batch, streaming, distributed storage, orchestration, and data-product foundations for backend engineers.

lessons.title: Introduction to Data Engineering
lessons.description: Data products, batch versus streaming, quality, and ownership.
lessons.concepts: Data engineering turns operational events into reliable, discoverable, and usable datasets. A pipeline needs an owner, schema, freshness target, quality checks, lineage, and recovery plan.
lessons.scenario: Turn order and payment events into a daily settlement dataset and a near-real-time operational view.
lessons.practice: Map sources, transformations, sinks, SLAs, and failure modes; define a small data contract before choosing tools.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the difference between an operational database and an analytical data product.
lessons.extension: Add a data-quality scorecard and a backfill policy.

lessons.title: Writing Efficient Queries: Part 1
lessons.description: Filtering, projection, joins, and query plans for analytical workloads.
lessons.concepts: Efficient queries reduce scanned data and unnecessary materialization. Select only needed columns, filter early when safe, understand join cardinality, and use the planner to validate assumptions.
lessons.scenario: Produce a merchant settlement report from partitioned order and payment data without scanning unrelated tenants or dates.
lessons.practice: Write a baseline query, inspect its plan, reduce scan volume, and test correctness against a small fixture.
lessons.evidence: You can tie a query change to bytes scanned, latency, and result correctness.
lessons.extension: Add a regression threshold for a scheduled report.

lessons.title: Writing Efficient Queries: Part 2
lessons.description: Partition pruning, skew, aggregation, and incremental computation.
lessons.concepts: Large queries fail through skew, shuffles, wide rows, and repeated full scans. Incremental processing and partition-aware writes reduce cost, but late data and corrections must be handled.
lessons.scenario: Recompute a merchant's daily metrics after late payment events without rebuilding the entire warehouse.
lessons.practice: Measure skew, choose a partition and clustering strategy, compare full and incremental aggregates, and define correction behavior.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the expensive stage and when incremental results may be temporarily incomplete.
lessons.extension: Add a watermark and a late-arrival reconciliation window.

lessons.title: Intro to Hadoop
lessons.description: Distributed storage and compute concepts in the Hadoop ecosystem.
lessons.concepts: Hadoop popularized separating distributed storage from parallel batch computation. The lasting concepts are data locality, replication, task failure, and processing data in parallel across nodes.
lessons.scenario: Process historical click or order events that are too large for a single machine while tolerating worker failure.
lessons.practice: Trace a file through distributed storage and a batch job, identify replication and locality decisions, and compare with object storage plus managed compute.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the problem Hadoop solves and why newer systems may be chosen today.
lessons.extension: Document a migration from legacy Hadoop jobs to a managed lakehouse workflow.

lessons.title: HDFS and MapReduce
lessons.description: Blocks, replication, map, shuffle, reduce, and failure recovery.
lessons.concepts: MapReduce makes data movement explicit: map produces keyed records, shuffle groups them, and reduce combines them. The shuffle is often the cost center, and reducers need a strategy for skew.
lessons.scenario: Count and aggregate events by merchant while one key is much hotter than the rest.
lessons.practice: Design the key, map and reduce functions, estimate shuffle volume, and handle malformed records without losing the whole job.
lessons.evidence: You can identify where data moves and why a bad key creates a straggler.
lessons.extension: Add a combiner or pre-aggregation and measure the reduction in shuffle data.

lessons.title: Introduction to Hive
lessons.description: SQL-on-files, schemas, partitions, and table ownership.
lessons.concepts: Hive provides a relational interface over distributed data, but file format, partition layout, schema evolution, and small-file behavior still determine performance and reliability.
lessons.scenario: Expose an event lake as partitioned tables for analysts while keeping raw immutable data available for replay.
lessons.practice: Define an external table, partition strategy, schema owner, and a query that avoids scanning unrelated partitions.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the difference between table metadata and underlying files.
lessons.extension: Add a compaction or small-file mitigation runbook.

lessons.title: Advanced Features of Hive
lessons.description: Partitioning, bucketing, joins, schema evolution, and warehouse operations.
lessons.concepts: Advanced warehouse design is about predictable access and controlled change. Bucketing can help specific joins, while schema evolution must preserve old readers and historical meaning.
lessons.scenario: Optimize a recurring customer-activity report and add a nullable field without breaking downstream consumers.
lessons.practice: Compare partition and bucket choices, test a schema change, and document table statistics and retention.
lessons.evidence: You can explain which optimization is workload-specific and how a consumer discovers a schema change.
lessons.extension: Add a data catalog entry with lineage and quality ownership.

lessons.title: Basics of Spark
lessons.description: Driver, executors, transformations, actions, and resilient computation.
lessons.concepts: Spark builds a logical plan and executes distributed transformations when an action is requested. Partition count, serialization, memory, and shuffle behavior matter more than the API surface alone.
lessons.scenario: Clean a large event dataset and compute daily aggregates while one executor is lost during the job.
lessons.practice: Trace a lazy transformation graph, choose an action, observe partitions, and explain how recomputation works.
lessons.evidence: You can distinguish a transformation from an action and identify when a shuffle occurs.
lessons.extension: Add a checkpoint or persisted dataset only when reuse justifies the storage cost.
lessons.reference: Apache Spark Documentation: RDD Programming Guide

lessons.title: Spark Programming
lessons.description: DataFrames, schemas, joins, aggregations, and job structure.
lessons.concepts: A Spark job should have a clear input contract, typed or validated transformations, bounded output, and metrics. Avoid collecting large data to the driver and make skew visible.
lessons.scenario: Build a batch job that creates a tenant-safe settlement dataset from events and writes partitioned output.
lessons.practice: Define the schema, implement transformations, test a small fixture, inspect the plan, and run a failure or skew scenario.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the job's stages and why the driver remains bounded.
lessons.extension: Add a data-quality quarantine output for malformed records.
lessons.reference: Apache Spark Documentation: SQL Programming Guide

lessons.title: Structured API - PySpark
lessons.description: Declarative schemas, expressions, and typed data transformations.
lessons.concepts: Structured APIs allow the engine to optimize a logical plan, but correctness still depends on explicit schemas, null behavior, and deterministic transformations.
lessons.scenario: Transform semi-structured AI extraction results into a typed dataset with rejected records separated from valid facts.
lessons.practice: Define schemas, handle nulls explicitly, compare inferred and declared schemas, and test nested field transformations.
lessons.evidence: You can explain how schema choices affect both correctness and optimization.
lessons.extension: Add a schema registry or versioned manifest for downstream consumers.

lessons.title: PySpark Operations
lessons.description: Joins, windows, UDF trade-offs, caching, and output layout.
lessons.concepts: PySpark code can hide distributed costs. Prefer native expressions over Python UDFs when possible, control join strategy, and cache only data reused within a measured job.
lessons.scenario: Calculate latest payment status per order and detect duplicate provider events at scale.
lessons.practice: Use window functions, compare a native expression with a UDF, inspect a join plan, and tune output partitioning.
lessons.evidence: You can identify a Python boundary or shuffle that drives cost and prove the result remains correct.
lessons.extension: Add a benchmark fixture that runs in CI with a small but representative skew.

lessons.title: Introduction to Streaming
lessons.description: Events, time, delivery, watermarks, and state.
lessons.concepts: Streaming systems process unbounded data. Event time, processing time, late data, replay, and state retention determine whether a result is trustworthy.
lessons.scenario: Update order metrics as events arrive out of order and allow a bounded delay before closing a daily window.
lessons.practice: Define event and processing timestamps, choose a watermark, model duplicates, and state what happens after a restart.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the difference between at-least-once input and exactly-once business effects.
lessons.extension: Add a replay command that rebuilds a window from immutable events.

lessons.title: Apache Spark Streaming
lessons.description: Structured Streaming queries, checkpoints, sinks, and triggers.
lessons.concepts: Structured Streaming turns a declarative query into a long-running job. Checkpoints, output mode, trigger interval, and sink idempotency form the recovery contract.
lessons.scenario: Aggregate payment events into a live merchant dashboard and write results to a durable sink.
lessons.practice: Configure a checkpoint, choose output mode, test a restart, and verify duplicate input handling.
lessons.evidence: You can explain what the checkpoint stores and when a sink can safely accept retries.
lessons.extension: Add a backpressure metric and a controlled pause/resume procedure.

lessons.title: Advanced Spark Streaming
lessons.description: Stateful operations, joins, late data, and operational tuning.
lessons.concepts: Stateful streams need bounded state, cleanup, and a plan for late or corrupt events. Stream-stream joins and aggregations should be constrained by time or keys.
lessons.scenario: Correlate order and payment events arriving on different streams while keeping state within an explicit retention window.
lessons.practice: Define watermarks and join windows, inject late events, observe state growth, and test recovery from a checkpoint.
lessons.evidence: You can explain when an event is too late and how the system reports incomplete or corrected results.
lessons.extension: Add a reconciliation stream for events outside the normal watermark.

lessons.title: Additional Streaming Services: Bringing It All Together
lessons.description: Brokers, schemas, processors, sinks, and end-to-end contracts.
lessons.concepts: A streaming architecture is a chain of contracts. Event schema, partition key, retention, consumer ownership, replay, and dead-letter behavior should be designed together.
lessons.scenario: Publish application events through Kafka, process them with Spark, write a warehouse table, and update an operational read model.
lessons.practice: Draw the end-to-end path, choose schema and key policies, test a consumer restart, and define replay without duplicating side effects.
lessons.evidence: You can trace an event from producer to sink and identify each point where data can be delayed or lost.
lessons.extension: Add lineage metadata and a per-stage freshness dashboard.

lessons.title: Modern Data Architectures
lessons.description: Lake, warehouse, lakehouse, serving layers, and data contracts.
lessons.concepts: Modern architectures separate raw immutable data, curated analytical tables, and low-latency serving views. The right shape depends on governance, freshness, cost, and consumer needs.
lessons.scenario: Design a platform for operational analytics, ML features, and customer-facing search without allowing each consumer to build an inconsistent copy.
lessons.practice: Map data products, ownership, storage layers, quality gates, and serving paths; call out the source of truth for each fact.
lessons.evidence: You can describe how data moves and why a layer exists.
lessons.extension: Add a contract-change process and a lineage view for a critical metric.

lessons.title: AWS Services for Data Engineering
lessons.description: Object storage, catalog, compute, streaming, query, and security choices.
lessons.concepts: Managed services reduce undifferentiated operations but create integration and cost decisions. Choose services from latency, scale, format, governance, and recovery requirements.
lessons.scenario: Build an AWS data path using S3 for raw data, a catalog, distributed processing, and a query layer with tenant-aware access.
lessons.practice: Map each requirement to one service, define IAM boundaries, encryption and retention, and identify a local development substitute.
lessons.evidence: You can explain what each managed service contributes and what remains your responsibility.
lessons.extension: Add cost allocation tags and a lifecycle policy for raw and curated data.

lessons.title: Data Modelling
lessons.description: Facts, dimensions, events, grain, slowly changing attributes, and analytical keys.
lessons.concepts: Analytical models make a row's grain explicit. Facts record measurable events, dimensions provide context, and slowly changing attributes require a choice about historical meaning.
lessons.scenario: Model order revenue by merchant, product, day, and region while preserving the merchant region at the time of purchase.
lessons.practice: Declare the grain, design fact and dimension tables, choose surrogate or natural keys, and test a late dimension change.
lessons.evidence: You can identify double-counting risk and explain which historical value a report should show.
lessons.extension: Add a semantic metric definition for revenue and settlement.

lessons.title: Orchestrating Data Pipelines
lessons.description: DAGs, dependencies, retries, idempotency, and backfills.
lessons.concepts: Orchestration is about making work observable and repeatable. A task should have inputs, outputs, retry policy, timeout, ownership, and a recovery or backfill path.
lessons.scenario: Schedule a daily settlement pipeline that depends on raw ingestion, quality checks, transformation, and publication.
lessons.practice: Draw the DAG, make tasks idempotent, define retry and alert policy, and run a historical backfill without overwriting corrected facts.
lessons.evidence: You can explain the state of a failed run and the safe next action.
lessons.extension: Add a run ledger and a freshness SLO.

lessons.title: Orchestration Continued
lessons.description: Sensors, dynamic tasks, deployment, and operational recovery.
lessons.concepts: Complex pipelines need bounded dynamic work, dependency checks, concurrency limits, and a deployment strategy that does not silently rerun expensive tasks.
lessons.scenario: Process one partition per tenant or date while limiting concurrency and skipping partitions that are already complete.
lessons.practice: Add dependency sensors, run-level idempotency, a concurrency cap, and a resume path after a worker failure.
lessons.evidence: You can show how an operator retries one safe task instead of restarting the entire DAG.
lessons.extension: Add a dry-run backfill planner and a cost estimate.

lessons.title: Distributed Coordination
lessons.description: Leases, leader election, locks, and coordination failure.
lessons.concepts: Coordination primitives have expiry, ownership, and split-brain behavior. A lock is not a substitute for an idempotent operation or a durable source of truth.
lessons.scenario: Only one pipeline coordinator may publish a daily partition while workers process independent shards.
lessons.practice: Define lease ownership and renewal, simulate a coordinator pause, and make publication idempotent after a takeover.
lessons.evidence: You can explain what happens when the owner disappears and why fencing or version checks may be required.
lessons.extension: Add a reconciliation task that detects overlapping or missing partition ownership.

lessons.title: Load Balancing
lessons.description: Data-worker placement, skew, throughput, and fairness.
lessons.concepts: Data workloads need balanced partitions and bounded workers. A fast worker does not help if one partition contains most records or a downstream sink has lower capacity.
lessons.scenario: Distribute tenant partitions across workers while one enterprise tenant is much larger than the rest.
lessons.practice: Measure partition sizes, split hot partitions, set concurrency, and verify downstream backpressure.
lessons.evidence: You can identify whether the bottleneck is compute, shuffle, storage, or the sink.
lessons.extension: Add adaptive partitioning with a reproducible threshold.

lessons.title: Data Pillars
lessons.description: Quality, governance, privacy, lineage, availability, and discoverability.
lessons.concepts: A trustworthy data product is accurate enough for its purpose, fresh enough for its SLA, secure, discoverable, and recoverable. Quality checks should be tied to actions, not only dashboards.
lessons.scenario: Publish a customer-facing settlement metric with ownership, lineage, freshness, privacy classification, and a correction path.
lessons.practice: Define quality dimensions, checks, alerts, access policy, retention, and a data incident process.
lessons.evidence: You can explain who owns a bad number and how a consumer learns whether it is safe to use.
lessons.extension: Create a lightweight data contract template for future FDE and backend projects.

lessons.title: Data Engineering Capstone
lessons.description: End-to-end batch and streaming platform design with evidence.
lessons.concepts: The capstone should produce a reliable data product, not a collection of disconnected jobs. Connect ingestion, storage, transformation, serving, quality, lineage, orchestration, and recovery.
lessons.scenario: Build an order and payment platform that supports daily settlement, live operations, and a replayable correction path.
lessons.practice: Write contracts and SLAs, implement a representative pipeline, inject late and duplicate events, measure cost and freshness, and present the recovery runbook.
lessons.evidence: You can trace a business metric to source events and demonstrate how an operator repairs a failed or late pipeline.
lessons.extension: Add a design review that compares the first architecture with the simplest version you would ship next.

authored_content.01-intro-to-lld:
# Lesson 1 — Intro to LLD for Scalable & AI-Ready Systems

## Concepts Covered
### High-Level Design vs. Low-Level Design
System design operates at two altitudes: infrastructure and code. High-Level Design (HLD) answers what components exist and how they connect — load balancers, application servers, databases, caches, message queues. It is a bird's-eye view of the system, deliberately silent on internals. Low-Level Design (LLD) answers how each component is actually written in code. The critical realization is that every infrastructure layer is itself just software. A load balancer is code that reads requests, applies a routing algorithm (round-robin, least-connections, ip-hash), and forwards them. A database is code that handles query parsing, storage engines, indexing, and transaction management. Once HLD has decided what to build, LLD governs how we write that code: maintainably (a teammate can read, modify, and extend it without breaking adjacent behaviour), extensibly (new requirements don't trigger rewrites of existing logic), and reusably (a payment abstraction written once plugs into checkout, refunds, and subscriptions without duplication). The gap between adding a new payment provider taking a day versus three weeks with regressions is an LLD question.

### Procedural Architecture vs. Object-Oriented Domain Entities
In Procedural style, functions are the active concept and data structs are passive — the puppeteer and the puppets. A `Trip` struct with fields `driverId`, `passengerId`, and `status` can be mutated by `updateTripStatus(trip, "CANCELLED")`, by direct assignment `trip.status = "COMPLETED"`, or by any function across the entire codebase holding a reference. As the system grows across hundreds of files and dozens of engineers, tracing which function corrupted a status field becomes an investigation, not a lookup. OOP resolves this by making entities the primary cognitive unit — a `Trip` object owns its state and exposes controlled methods that enforce business rules at the point where the data lives. Real OOP keeps behaviour close to the data it governs: state transitions belong in the entity, not in an anemic service class that reaches into getters and setters. Service classes coordinate across entities; entities govern their own state.

## Practical Backend Scenario
A passenger requests a ride and a driver accepts. While the driver is en route, the passenger attempts to cancel. The caller that needs the display string receives it in one call without knowing the internal format or length.

# Lesson 4 — OOP-3: Polymorphism, Abstract Classes & Interfaces

## Concepts Covered

Polymorphism originates from the Greek roots *poly* (multiple) and *morph* (form): the core object-oriented principle where a single entity, interface, or method call can take on multiple concrete forms at runtime and compile time. Without polymorphism, software systems become rigid and brittle — adding a new vehicle type or payment gateway would require modifying and rewriting dispatch logic across every calling service.

Object-oriented polymorphism divides into two primary mechanisms:
### Runtime Polymorphism (Dynamic Dispatch)
Implemented via **method overriding**, where a subclass provides its own specific implementation of a method declared in its parent class. Dynamic dispatch is governed by a fundamental dual-perspective rule:
   - **Reference type** $\rightarrow$ determines which methods you **CAN** call (enforced strictly by the compiler at compile time).
   - **Actual object type** $\rightarrow$ determines which implementation **RUNS** (dispatched dynamically by the JVM at runtime).
   When `Vehicle v = new Cab(); v.calculateFare();` executes, the compiler verifies that `Vehicle` declares `calculateFare()`, but the JVM dispatches execution to `Cab.calculateFare()`.
### Compile-Time Polymorphism (Static Resolution)
Implemented via **method overloading**, where multiple methods in the same class share the exact same method name but differ in their parameter signatures (parameter count, parameter types, or parameter order). The compiler resolves the exact method to invoke before execution. Return type alone, access modifiers, or variable parameter names cannot differentiate overloads because the compiler cannot resolve call sites based on discarded return values. Static methods can be overloaded, but cannot be overridden (they are hidden). Operator overloading is not supported in Java.

### Abstraction as Code
The `abstract` keyword represents an idea, concept, or blueprint rather than a concrete instance. A generic base class like `Vehicle` represents a thought; concrete entities like `Cab`, `Auto`, and `Bike` represent physical vehicles. Declaring `public abstract class Vehicle` prevents direct instantiation (`new Vehicle()` is a compile-time error) while enforcing implementation obligations on subclasses through abstract methods such as `public abstract double getBaseFare();`.

### The Diamond Problem and Interfaces
Multiple class inheritance creates structural ambiguity when two parent classes (`A` and `B`) extend a common base class and override the same method — a child class `C` inheriting from both cannot determine which parent implementation to execute. Java solves this by prohibiting multiple class inheritance, using `interface` instead. An interface is a pure capability contract across unrelated class hierarchies (`class C implements A, B`). Interface fields are implicitly `public static final`, and methods define capability contracts (expanded to include `default` methods in Java 8+).

### Composition vs. Inheritance — The Three-Question Design Test
Inheritance couples classes tightly. The decision framework for choosing the correct design tool is:

| Relationship Type | Question | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| IS A TYPE OF | Does X inherit structural identity and shared mechanics from Y? | `extends` / abstract class |
| CAN DO | Does X possess capability Y across unrelated class families? | `implements` / interface |
| HAS A | Does X contain Y as an internal collaborator or component? | composition / private field |

## Practical Backend Scenario

A ride-hailing dispatch fleet service manages multimodal transport options across a metropolitan network. The system defines an abstract base class `Vehicle` that encapsulates shared state (`vehicleId`, `driverName`) and exposes a template method `calculateFare(int distanceKm) { return distanceKm * getBaseFare(); }` with an abstract `getBaseFare()`. Subclasses specialize only their per-kilometer pricing: `Cab` returns 15.0, `Auto` returns 10.0, and `Bike` returns 5.0.

The dispatch service layer `CabBookingService` overloads `bookRide()` to support multiple client workflows: `bookRide(String pickup, String drop)`, `bookRide(String pickup, String drop, int rideTimeMinutes)`, and `bookRide(String pickup, String drop, int rideTimeMinutes, Coupon coupon)`. When dispatching a trip, the fleet orchestrator iterates over a polymorphic `List<Vehicle> fleet`. Calling `v.calculateFare(distanceKm)` dynamically executes each vehicle's specialized rate without any `instanceof` inspection. Payment processing is decoupled using a `PaymentGateway` interface (`CAN DO`), allowing `RazorpayAdapter` or `StripeAdapter` to be composed into the booking workflow (`HAS A`).

## Practice Loop

1. Write an abstract `Vehicle` class with private fields (`vehicleId`, `driverName`), a concrete `calculateFare(int km)` method, and an abstract `getBaseFare()` method.
2. Create concrete subclasses `Cab`, `Auto`, and `Bike` extending `Vehicle`, implementing `getBaseFare()` and adding `@Override` annotations.
3. Implement `CabBookingService` with overloaded `bookRide()` methods demonstrating parameter count and type variations.
4. Construct a `List<Vehicle>` containing a `Cab`, `Auto`, and `Bike`; iterate through the collection and invoke `calculateFare(10)`, observing dynamic method dispatch at runtime.
5. Create a `PaymentGateway` interface (`CAN DO`) with `processPayment(double amount)` and compose it as a private field (`HAS A`) inside `CabBookingService`, verifying that payment changes require zero modifications to the vehicle hierarchy.

## Evidence of Understanding

You can articulate the dual-perspective rule of polymorphism — reference type governs compile-time method accessibility while actual heap type governs runtime execution. You can explain why return types cannot differentiate overloaded methods, demonstrate how abstract classes enforce subclass obligations, and explain how interfaces prevent the Diamond Problem. You can apply the Three-Question Design Test to justify choosing composition over inheritance.

## Suggested Extension

# Lesson 5 — OOP-4: Library Management System Lab

## Concepts Covered

This lab synthesizes all four core pillars of Object-Oriented Programming — **Encapsulation**, **Abstraction**, **Inheritance**, and **Polymorphism** — by constructing a comprehensive Library Management System (LMS) from scratch.

### Abstraction and System Blueprinting
Abstraction models complex systems as interacting, bounded entities while hiding implementation mechanics. In the LMS architecture, abstraction operates across two distinct constructs:
- **Abstract Classes:** `User` and `Book` serve as abstract base blueprints that cannot be instantiated directly. They define shared state and contract obligations for concrete specializations.
- **Interfaces:** `Lendable` serves as a pure capability contract (`lend`, `returnItem`, `isAvailable`) that attaches lending behavior across disparate entity hierarchies without imposing an unnatural inheritance tree.

### Inheritance and Constructor Chaining
Inheritance shares structural identity across the domain (`Member IS-A User`, `Librarian IS-A User`). When a subclass object is instantiated (`new Member("Asha", "asha@email.com")`), Java enforces strict constructor ordering:
1. `Member` constructor is invoked.
2. `super(...)` passes execution immediately to `User`.
3. `User` initializes shared identity fields, generates a unique ID, and increments `totalUsers`.
4. Control returns to `Member` for subclass-specific field initialization.

### Class-Level Rules with static and final
- `static` fields (`idCounter`, `totalUsers`) belong to the class itself, maintaining a single shared copy in memory across all instances. `getTotalUsers()` is a `static` method callable on `User` directly.
- `final` instance fields (`final String userId`) are assigned exactly once during constructor execution and cannot be reassigned afterwards.
- `static final` constants (`static final int MAX_BORROW_LIMIT = 5`) define immutable, class-wide policy constants.

### The Three Constructor Types and Copy Semantics
- **Default Constructor:** Initializes objects with safe, deterministic initial values.
- **Parameterized Constructor:** Provides complete field initialization at creation time.
- **Copy Constructor:** Creates an independent object cloned from an existing instance. In the LMS, a copied user invokes `generateUniqueId()` and increments `totalUsers` rather than copying `other.userId` directly, preserving the strict invariant that all users possess distinct IDs. Similarly, a copied book resets `isAvailable = true`.

### Polymorphic Execution Without instanceof
In `Book.lend(User user)`, the method executes:
```java
if (isAvailable && user.canBorrowBooks()) {
    isAvailable = false;
    return true;
}
```
`user.canBorrowBooks()` executes polymorphically: for a `Member`, it checks `borrowedBooksCount < MAX_BORROW_LIMIT`; for a `Librarian`, it returns `true` unconditionally. No `instanceof` type checks are required.

### The Access Modifiers Table (Why Every LMS Field Is private)
| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package | Subclass | Everywhere |
|----------|------------|--------------|----------|------------|
| `private` | yes | no | no | no |
| default | yes | yes | no | no |
| `protected` | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `public` | yes | yes | yes | yes |

Every entity field in the LMS (`userId`, `borrowedBooksCount`, `isAvailable`) stays
`private`, with access only through public getters and controlled mutator methods. This is
why `Member.borrowedBooksCount` cannot be touched directly by `Book.lend()` — the two
classes are not in an inheritance relationship, so `protected` would not even help; the
field must go through `Member`'s own public methods.

### Why Book.lend() Never Calls incrementBorrowCount() Directly
`LibraryManagementSystem.lendBook()` delegates in two separate steps: first `book.lend(member)`,
then — only if that succeeded — `member.incrementBorrowCount()`. `Book.lend()` itself never
calls `incrementBorrowCount()`. This separation is deliberate: a `Book` should not need to
know how a `Member` tracks its own borrow count internally, and a `Member`'s counting logic
should not need to know how a `Book` decides availability. Each class stays responsible for
exactly one piece of state, and the orchestrator (`LibraryManagementSystem`) is the only
place that knows both steps must happen together.

### The IS-A Test for This Domain
Every inheritance relationship in the LMS should pass a simple intuition check: does
"Child IS-A Parent" read naturally as a sentence? "Member IS-A User" and "Librarian IS-A
User" both read naturally, confirming `extends` is the right tool. If a relationship does
not read naturally as IS-A, composition (a field reference) is the correct choice instead,
not inheritance.

## Practical Backend Scenario

The Library Management System is structured across three core progressive milestones:

**Milestone 1 — User Hierarchy & Identity Management:**
Implement abstract base class `User` with private fields (`userId`, `name`, `contactInfo`), a `static int idCounter`, and a `static int totalUsers`. Implement constructor chaining across default, parameterized, and copy constructors. Implement `Member` with private `borrowedBooksCount`, `static final int MAX_BORROW_LIMIT = 5`, and concrete `canBorrowBooks()`. Implement `Librarian` with unrestricted borrowing privileges.

**Milestone 2 — Lending Architecture & Capability Attachment:**
Define the `Lendable` interface declaring `boolean lend(User user)`, `void returnItem(User user)`, and `boolean isAvailable()`. Implement abstract base `Book` implementing `Lendable`, encapsulating private fields (`bookId`, `title`, `author`, `isAvailable`). Create concrete subclasses `TextBook` (with subject/edition fields) and `NovelBook` (with genre fields) overriding `displayBookDetails()`. Non-lendable reference items (`Journal`, `Encyclopedia`) extend `Book` but do not implement `Lendable` (or throw unsupported operation exceptions), maintaining clean separation between what an item IS versus what it CAN DO.

**Milestone 3 — Full Management System Coordination:**
Build the central orchestrator `LibraryManagementSystem` managing `List<Book>` and `List<User>`. Implement methods for `registerUser(User u)`, `addBook(Book b)`, `lendBook(String bookId, String userId)`, and `returnBook(String bookId, String userId)`. Implement overloaded book search methods: `searchBooks(String titleQuery)` and `searchBooks(String titleQuery, String itemType)`. Implement `displayRegisteredUsers()` iterating polymorphically over `List<User>` and invoking `u.displayDashboard()`.

## Practice Loop

1. Build Milestone 1: Create `User`, `Member`, and `Librarian`. Verify that creating three users and one copied member increments `User.getTotalUsers()` to 4 and assigns 4 distinct unique IDs.
2. Build Milestone 2: Define `Lendable`, `Book`, `TextBook`, and `NovelBook`. Verify `TextBook` and `NovelBook` inherit lending logic and implement specific details.
3. Build Milestone 3: Implement `LibraryManagementSystem` coordinating user registration, catalog storage, and borrowing transactions.
4. Test borrowing invariants: Register a `Member`, borrow 5 books successfully, and assert that the 6th borrow attempt fails. Register a `Librarian` and assert that borrowing beyond 5 succeeds.
5. Test encapsulation boundaries: Ensure `Member.borrowedBooksCount` cannot be mutated directly by `Book.lend()`, but only through controlled helper methods `incrementBorrowCount()` and `decrementBorrowCount()`.
6. Trace this exact sequence and predict how many `User` objects exist and how many unique
   IDs are generated:
   ```java
   Member asha = new Member("Asha", "asha@email.com");
   User copy = new Member(asha);
   System.out.println(asha.getUserId().equals(copy.getUserId()));
   ```
   (Two independent `Member` objects exist; the copy constructor must call
   `generateUniqueId()` rather than copying `asha`'s ID, so the printed result is `false`.)

## Evidence of Understanding

You can explain why `User` and `Book` are abstract classes, why copy constructors must generate fresh unique IDs and increment static instance counters, how `Book.lend()` relies on runtime polymorphism rather than `instanceof` checks, and how interfaces attach capabilities across class hierarchies without forcing unrelated entities into an artificial inheritance tree.

Add a `FinePolicy` strategy interface (`calculateFine(int overdueDays)`) with `StandardFinePolicy` (\$1/day) and `PremiumMemberFinePolicy` (first 3 days free), injecting the appropriate policy into `Member` at registration time.

# Lesson 6 — Concurrency 1: Processes, Threads & Context Switching

## Concepts Covered

Concurrent software execution requires understanding how operating systems allocate processing resources and memory at runtime.

### The Office / Company Metaphor
A running system is analogous to an office environment:
- **Company = Process:** A self-contained running program allocated its own physical floor space, address space in RAM, and OS resources.
- **Employees = Threads:** Lightweight execution units operating inside the process. Each employee has their own private notepad (Call Stack) and task bookmark (Program Counter), but all employees share the office desks, filing cabinets, and whiteboard (Heap Memory).
- **Managers = CPU Scheduler:** The decision-maker determining which employee works at a physical desk during each time slice.
- **Desks = CPU Cores:** The physical processing hardware where instructions actively advance.

### Diagnostic Questions — Concurrency vs. Parallelism
- *How many tasks are partially done simultaneously?*
- *How many tasks actively advance right now?*
- **Concurrency (Managing Many Things at Once):** A single-core CPU executing multiple tasks via rapid time-slicing. Multiple tasks are in various stages of completion, but only one task actively advances at any given instant.
- **Parallelism (Doing Many Things at Once):** Multi-core hardware running multiple tasks simultaneously. Multiple tasks are partially done AND multiple tasks actively advance at the exact same physical moment across separate cores.

### Five Real-World Anchors for the Office Metaphor
- **Process = browser tabs:** modern browsers run separate tabs in separate processes; one
  tab crashing does not take down the others, because each has its own isolated memory space.
- **Thread = a video game's internal workers:** one thread renders graphics, a second
  manages audio, a third reads controller input, and a fourth autosaves progress — all four
  share the same game state in memory but run independently.
- **CPU Scheduler = a web server under load:** when incoming requests outnumber the
  server's processing capacity, the scheduler decides execution order so no request starves
  while avoiding excessive switching overhead.
- **Context Switching = losing your place while studying:** pausing one subject to
  context-switch to another and back costs real time re-orienting yourself — time spent on
  logistics, not on the actual work. A CPU pays the same cost saving and restoring register
  state on every thread switch.
- **Runnable = handing off a written task:** a scheduled report defines *what* needs doing
  without specifying *which* employee performs it — exactly like handing a task description
  to whichever thread the scheduler assigns next.

### From Code to Process in Memory
- Source code $\rightarrow$ Compiled into an Executable on Disk (Program) $\rightarrow$ Loaded into RAM upon execution (Process).
- The OS tracks each process using a **Process Control Block (PCB)**, which stores `ProcessID`, `ProcessName`, `State` (Ready, Running, Blocked), `ExecutionTime`, `MemoryLimit`, `ResourcesAllocated`, and `LastLineExecuted` / register snapshots.
- Processes execute in isolated memory spaces; inter-process communication (IPC) requires heavy operating-system mechanisms.

### Threads — Lightweight Execution Units
- A **Thread** is the smallest unit of execution scheduled by the CPU.
- Every thread within a process owns an independent **Call Stack** (local variables, method frames) and **Program Counter (PC)**.
- All threads in the same process share the common **Heap**, static memory, and file descriptors. Communication between threads is instant via shared memory, but requires synchronization to prevent corruption.

### Context Switching & Scheduling Overhead
- When the CPU switches execution from Thread 1 to Thread 2, it saves Thread 1's register state, program counter, and stack pointer, and loads Thread 2's context.
- Context switching consumes CPU cycles and causes CPU cache line invalidation (cache thrashing). Excessive thread creation degrades throughput because the CPU spends more time switching contexts than executing application logic.

### Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for Multithreading in Java
1. *Think in terms of tasks to be completed in parallel, not raw threads.*
2. Create a dedicated task class implementing the `Runnable` functional interface.
3. Place execution logic inside the `public void run()` method.
4. Pass required parameters to the task object via its constructor.
5. Pass the task object to a new `Thread` instance: `Thread t = new Thread(task);`.
6. Invoke `t.start()`. *Critical rule:* Calling `t.run()` executes the method synchronously on the current thread without spawning a new execution thread. Calling `t.start()` registers the thread with the JVM/OS scheduler to begin concurrent execution.
7. Recognize that thread execution order is **non-deterministic** — the CPU scheduler controls thread execution timing.

## Practical Backend Scenario

A collaborative document processing engine (such as Google Docs or MS Word) runs as a single application process in RAM. Within this process, multiple concurrent threads operate over the shared in-memory document model:
- **Thread 1 (UI & Event Handling):** Captures real-time keyboard inputs, mouse clicks, and renders updates to the display buffer.
- **Thread 2 (Background Autosave):** Periodically serializes document state and flushes changes to persistent cloud storage every 30 seconds.
- **Thread 3 (Spell & Grammar Checking):** Tokenizes text in the background, cross-referencing dictionaries and grammar models without interrupting the user.
- **Thread 4 (Real-time Collaboration Sync):** Listens on WebSockets for incoming remote edits from other collaborators.

All threads share heap memory, allowing instant visibility of text buffer edits, while maintaining independent call stacks so that an I/O pause during cloud autosave never freezes the interactive UI thread.

1. Write a `NumberPrinterTask` implementing `Runnable` that takes an integer `number` via constructor and prints `number` along with `Thread.currentThread().getName()`.
2. In `main()`, spawn 10 threads running `NumberPrinterTask` for numbers 1 through 10 using `new Thread(task).start()`; run the program 5 times and observe the non-deterministic output sequence.
3. Replace `t.start()` with `t.run()` in the loop; observe that execution becomes strictly sequential (1..10) on the `main` thread, demonstrating that `run()` bypasses thread creation.
4. Implement a background `AutosaveTask` with a `while(true)` loop containing `Thread.sleep(2000)` and a print statement; run it concurrently alongside a main loop reading user input from `Scanner`.
5. Use an OS process monitor (`Task Manager`, `Activity Monitor`, or `jconsole`) to inspect live thread counts and CPU utilization while varying the number of active worker threads.

You can map the office metaphor to processes, threads, CPU schedulers, and cores. You can distinguish concurrency from parallelism using the two diagnostic questions. You can detail which memory segments are private to a thread (Stack, PC) versus shared across threads (Heap), explain context switching overhead, and demonstrate the mandatory SOP for creating and starting Java threads with `Runnable` and `start()`.

## Suggested Extension

Build a concurrent word frequency counter where a large text document is divided into 4 distinct text chunks, each processed by a separate `ChunkWordCounter` thread implementing `Runnable`, aggregating partial word counts into a shared reporting data structure.
